profiles.name: Arts Gowanus
profiles.seat: Community based arts organisation · Gowanus, Brooklyn
profiles.desc: Arts Gowanus at 543 Union Street in Gowanus. Gowanus Open Studios, art programming, the Arts Gowanus Fellowship, and advocacy for affordable artist studios in the Gowanus rezoning.
intro: Arts Gowanus has worked for the artists of Gowanus since 1996. In the words of its own mission, Arts Gowanus nurtures a diverse, inclusive creative community that welcomes all artists in the neighborhood, creating new spaces for art to bring people together, build a more vibrant community, and uplift the greater Gowanus area.

Arts Gowanus runs Gowanus Open Studios, which it calls Brooklyn’s largest celebration of local art, with more than 400 artists, businesses and venues opening their doors from Pacific Street to 19th Street and from Smith Street to Fifth Avenue. The 30th annual Open Studios is October 17 and 18, 2026.
Executive Director Johnny Thornton leads the organisation.
does: Arts Gowanus runs art programming and partnerships that raise the visibility of Gowanus artists across the city, the Arts Gowanus Fellowship, which covers a selected artist’s studio rent, and curatorial services.

On the Gowanus rezoning, Arts Gowanus negotiated a Community Benefits Agreement that secures roughly 120 subsidized artist studios across the development sites, starting at $20 a square foot a year, with one studio in each building reserved for a low income artist. The agreement also secures a 2,000 square foot community arts center with three residency studios, affordable in perpetuity.

Arts Gowanus works alongside the Gowanus Neighborhood Coalition for Justice, the Gowanus Oversight Task Force, GRACE and the Gowanus Improvement District. The office at 543 Union Street is zoned M1-4/R7-2 inside the Gowanus special district.

profiles.name: Fifth Avenue Committee
profiles.seat: Community based organisation · Park Slope and Gowanus, Brooklyn
profiles.desc: Fifth Avenue Committee at 621 DeGraw Street. Affordable housing, organizing, adult education and workforce development since 1978.
profiles.addr_note: Second office at 132 32nd Street, Suite 106, Brooklyn, NY 11232
intro: The Fifth Avenue Committee has been at this since 1978, and it is one of the few organisations in the district that does development, organizing and services at the same time rather than picking one. It reaches more than 6,500 low and moderate income New Yorkers a year.

Its stated aim is economic, social and racial justice, pursued through community-centred affordable housing, grassroots organizing, policy advocacy, and education and training. That combination is the point. An organisation that only builds housing does not have tenants organized; one that only organizes does not own anything.
The lot at 621 DeGraw is owned by FAC Center Local Development Corporation, which tells you something. They own the building they organize from.
does: On housing it builds and manages affordable and supportive housing, with a pipeline running to as many as 1,900 units, and it has done the unglamorous work too: gut renovations of small rental buildings, LEED Gold mixed-income developments, and a public library, a public park and five Pre-K classrooms folded into its projects.

On the ground it runs tenant counseling and organizing, foreclosure prevention and homebuyer counseling, and adult education including GED prep, English classes and digital literacy for over a thousand adults a year.
Workforce development runs through its affiliate Brooklyn Workforce Innovations. South Brooklyn Against Displacement is its organizing arm.

profiles.name: Friends of Fort Defiance
profiles.seat: Grassroots history and resiliency group · Red Hook, Brooklyn
profiles.desc: Friends of Fort Defiance, Red Hook, Brooklyn. A grassroots organization exploring Red Hook histories in dialogue with the future: research on the Revolutionary-era redoubt Fort Defiance, the Fort Defiance Street Museum on Coffey Street, Fort Defiance 250 and Brooklyn250, and concepts for a resiliency hub, flood mitigation and an urban forest.
profiles.addr_note: Fort Defiance Street Museum, 160 and 169 Coffey Street
intro: Friends of Fort Defiance is a grassroots organization exploring Red Hook histories in dialogue with the future. Formed in December 2024, the group researches the Revolutionary-era redoubt named Fort Defiance, designs a modular system for neighborhood-wide flood mitigation, and has drawn up a concept called Fort Defiance Park: a resiliency hub with a historic park overlay and an urban industrial campus.

The natural fortifications that once held back the British armada are now needed to hold back future floodwaters in Red Hook. Friends of Fort Defiance is fiscally sponsored by the Open Space Institute through its Citizen Action Program.
does: Fort Defiance 250. Friends of Fort Defiance is one of six partners leading Brooklyn250, the borough-wide commemoration of the 250th anniversary of the Battle of Brooklyn, alongside Green-Wood Cemetery, the Old Stone House, Brooklyn Public Library’s Center for Brooklyn History, Prospect Park Alliance and Fort Greene Park Conservancy. Brooklyn250 brings the Revolutionary history to life with free tours, exhibitions, performances, reenactments, panel discussions, book talks, family programs and a collectible then-and-now pamphlet and map, supported by $350,000 in state funding championed by Assemblymember Robert Carroll, Assemblymember Jo Anne Simon and State Senator Andrew Gounardes.

Fort Defiance 250 events so far. April 8, 2026: A Rebirthday Celebration of the Fort Named Defiance. May 21: The Tides of History, Fort Banter and the Climate Justice Action Plan in conversation, at the Waterfront Museum with Resilient Red Hook. August 22: Put Red Hook on the Historical Map, a panel at Valentino Park moderated by Greg Young of The Bowery Boys and co-presented with the Red Hook Business Alliance.

Fort Defiance Street Museum. Sidewalk galleries at 160 and 169 Coffey Street present archaeological findings and significant source materials about Fort Defiance, Red Hook Lane and the defense of New York Harbor in the campaign of 1776. Open between sunrise and midnight.

Three concepts. Fort Defiance Park, a resiliency hub with a historic park overlay and an urban industrial campus, drawn for an empty site that was part of a public visioning process (Friends of Fort Defiance is not affiliated with the site owners); the Stormbreaker Network, a modular design system for neighborhood-wide flood mitigation; and Liberty Forest, a meandering urban forest connecting Brooklyn Bridge Park and Fort Defiance Park through the Brooklyn Marine Terminal.

History. A growing collection of maps, paintings, writings and overlays on Red Hook’s natural, industrial and revolutionary histories, from the 1766 Montresor map of Red Hook and Governors Island to a 2024 topographic change analysis for Fort Defiance by Eymund Diegel, plus two cannonballs found in a neighbor’s backyard that the group is working with a scientist to attribute to the fort.
Engage. Friends of Fort Defiance tables at events to keep developing the concepts in community, takes volunteers, and invites feedback or new ideas drawn on their template.

Old Stone House, Green-Wood Cemetery, Center for Brooklyn History, Prospect Park Alliance, Fort Greene Park Conservancy

profiles.name: Gowanus Canal Conservancy
profiles.desc: Gowanus Canal Conservancy at the Old American Can Factory, 248 Third Street. Stewardship of the canal watershed, the Lowlands Nursery, the Green Team and the Tree Network.
profiles.addr: The Old American Can Factory, 248 Third Street
profiles.addr_note: Third Street at Third Avenue. The city files the lot as 361 3 Avenue
intro: The Gowanus Canal Conservancy is the group that has done the work on the canal since 2006, out of the Old American Can Factory: volunteers in the rain gardens and tree pits, students in the watershed, and staff at every meeting where the canal’s future gets decided, including ours. On the rezoning they were ahead of everyone, with a plan for the waterfront before the City had one, and they’re on the Oversight Task Force now making sure the open space and stormwater commitments get built.

Andrea Parker and her excellent team has run and met the moment for over a decade, and her team includes CB6 member Aurelia Casey. If you want to see what stewardship looks like in practice, go to the Salt Lot on a volunteer day.
does: GCC runs the Lowlands Nursery, growing native urban-adapted plants and selling them to residents, institutions and landscape designers, with proceeds going back into education and stewardship.

GCC runs the Gowanus Green Team, paid high school apprentices doing conservation work, and the Gowanus Tree Network, which trains neighbours as Citizen Pruners to look after the street trees on their own blocks.

The Conservancy works out of the Old American Can Factory, a three storey 1890 complex at Third Street and Third Avenue that now houses artists, makers and non-profits. The lot is zoned M1-4/R7X inside the Gowanus special district, the mixed use zoning the 2021 rezoning brought in.

profiles.name: The Old Stone House
profiles.seat: Historic house and Washington Park · Park Slope and Gowanus, Brooklyn
profiles.desc: The Old Stone House at 336 3rd Street in Washington Park. What it runs, how to reach it, and the ground it stands on.
profiles.addr_note: Between 4th and 5th Avenues, inside Washington Park
intro: The Old Stone House sits where history actually happened, in the middle of Washington Park, between 3rd and 4th Streets and between 4th and 5th Avenues. It runs family programs, arts and cultural events, addresses neighborhood issues, and manages the gardens; aka it’s a great institution.

A house that has grown by leaps and bounds in the decades since I was in middle school in the late 1990s. Much of that is down to Executive Director Kim Maier, who has built it into a place that honors the past, lives in the present, and improves the future.

The building, the actual house, is a reconstruction of the 1699 Vechte-Cortelyou House, on land taken from the Lenape as early as 1639. It stands in Washington Park on the border of Park Slope and Gowanus, marking the site of the original Dutch farmstead and the culminating engagement of the Battle of Brooklyn in 1776. It is also the birthplace of the Brooklyn Dodgers back when there were trolley’s to dodge. It is a Historic House Trust of New York City site and rightly resides on the National Register of Historic Places.
does: An interactive exhibit on the largest battle of the Revolutionary War and what living in Brooklyn was like from 1776 to 1783. Contemporary shows by emerging artists. Gardens of native and useful plants. School visits and field trips. Concerts, readings, lectures and theater, including Piper Theatre. A summer camp. And the playground, courts, turf field and dog run that make up JJ Byrne.

profiles.name: Van Alen Institute
profiles.desc: Van Alen Institute at 303 Bond Street in Gowanus. What it does, how to reach it, and the lot it stands on. Brooklyn Community Board 6 holds its meetings there.
profiles.addr_note: Between Union and Sackett Streets, on the west bank of the canal
intro: The Van Alen Institute has been at this since 1894, which makes it older than the Gowanus rezoning by about a century and a quarter. It works on community-led urban design, the premise being that the people who live somewhere know things about it that a designer parachuting in does not.

What that means in practice is that it builds coalitions across designers, residents and city agencies, then backs them with scoping, hands-on guidance and seed money. It is explicit that its work is about power imbalances in how cities get made, and it partners with historically disinvested communities rather than the ones already well served.

It moved to 303 Bond Street in Gowanus, on the west bank of the canal, inside the area the 2021 rezoning reshaped. Brooklyn Community Board 6 holds our meetings there, which is a good arrangement for everyone: an organisation devoted to community-led design hosting the body whose whole job is community input on land use.
does: Van Alen runs design competitions, public space projects, research and fellowships. The through line is that it does not just publish a report and leave; it puts money and staff behind the ideas it generates and stays with them.

For CB6 the relevant thing is proximity and subject matter. This is a district with a Superfund canal, a major rezoning still being built out, a waterfront terminal decision coming, and six historic districts. An institution working on how communities shape the built environment is useful to have on the block.

profiles.name: Carroll Park
profiles.desc: Carroll Park. 375 Court Street, Brooklyn
intro: One of the oldest parks in Brooklyn, in three parts: an asphalt yard with basketball hoops and a baseball and kickball diamond for older kids, a play area for older and younger kids with a compass-shaped spray shower, and a shady section with seating and public bathrooms.

Brooklyn's third-oldest park. It is named for Charles Carroll (1737-1832), a signer of the Declaration of Independence who served in the Continental Congress and as a U.S. Senator from Maryland. Carroll Street carries his name too.

It began in the late 1840s as a private garden, soon after surveyor Richard Butt laid out much of what is now the Carroll Gardens Historic District. The City of Brooklyn bought the land for a public park in 1853.
Around 1870 it got drainage, new walks and a children's playground. Later rebuilds in the 1890s, 1930s and 1960s added playgrounds and more room for active play.

In 1994 a $1.3 million reconstruction funded by Borough President Howard Golden replanted the park, reorganized the play areas and put back cast-iron gates and fencing that echo the neighborhood's brownstones. The bronze and granite World War I Soldiers and Sailors Monument (1920) by sculptor Eugene H. Morahan was conserved in the same project.
The Committee to Improve Carroll Park, formed in 1975, works with NYC Parks on programs, upkeep and care of the park.

profiles.name: Harold Ickes Playground
profiles.desc: Harold Ickes Playground. 100 Hamilton Avenue, Brooklyn
intro: The City acquired this land between 1940 and 1945 for the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel, now the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel. Robert Moses had wanted a bridge; after President Roosevelt had the Army refuse permits for it, a tunnel was built instead, begun in 1940 and finished in 1950. A tunnel ventilation shaft sits in a corner of the playground.
In 2024 Parks turned an underused asphalt lot here into Red Hook's first BMX and skate park, with a playground, climbing boulders and open space for parkour.

Named for Harold L. Ickes (1874-1952), Secretary of the Interior in Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal cabinet, who oversaw the public works program that built parks, highways, public buildings and the Hoover Dam.

profiles.name: Bartel-Pritchard Square
profiles.desc: Bartel-Pritchard Square.
intro: A traffic circle at the southwest entrance to Prospect Park, Prospect Park West and 15th Street. Inside are a planting bed, benches and a polished black granite war memorial dedicated in 1965 "For Valor and Sacrifice."

The Board of Aldermen named the square on April 10, 1923, for two Brooklyn friends, Emil Bartel (1895-1918) of 251 Windsor Place and William Pritchard of Linden Street in Bushwick. Both joined the National Guard's 13th Regiment, served in the 59th Coast Artillery, and were killed in combat in France in World War I.
In 1965 the Patrick J. Devaney Post #964 put up the granite monument to the men of the community who died defending the country.

profiles.name: Red Hook Recreation Area
profiles.desc: Red Hook Recreation Area. 825 Henry Street, Brooklyn
intro: Handball, basketball and soccer, a busy playground, an Olympic-size outdoor pool in summer, a running track and a recreation center with cardio equipment, weights and exercise classes.
The City acquired the first piece of this land on October 10, 1913, for freight rail terminals. It was assigned to Parks on June 27, 1934, and the other parcels came to Parks between 1935 and 1947.

Landscape architect Gilmore D. Clarke laid out the original plan under Parks Commissioner Robert Moses. Then called the Red Hook Recreation Center, it opened on August 12, 1936; the New York Times reported more than 40,000 people, many of them children, cheering Mayor Fiorello La Guardia at the opening.

Parks' history of the site ties it to Red Hook's story: the docks of the Atlantic and Erie Basins, the Red Hook Houses (opened in 1938 for dockworkers' families), the 1946 Gowanus Expressway that cut Red Hook off from the rest of Brooklyn, and a population that fell from 18,575 in 1960 to 10,485 in 1980.
Today it holds paths, benches, handball courts, baseball fields, a soccer and football field, picnic tables and the Sol Goldman Pool next door.

The City acquired the two parcels that make up the park in three phases between 1941 and 1947. A 1967 local law named the larger part for Vincent J. DiMattina; the smaller part was left without a name.
Parks added a dog run to the larger part in 2001 and improved the play areas. In 2015 the DiMattina Dog Run was rebuilt and enlarged with separate areas for large and small dogs.

DiMattina (1915-1966) started on the Brooklyn waterfront at 16, served as a Navy Seabee deep-sea diver in the South Pacific in World War II, became a lawyer in 1954, was New York State Commander of the Veterans of Foreign Wars in the 1960s, and was active in civic and church life in Carroll Gardens.

The block of Warren, Hoyt, Baltic and Smith Streets has been run jointly by Parks and the Board of Education since 1967, serving the Cobble Hill High School of American Studies and the neighborhood. For almost 30 years parts of it were a teachers' parking lot and a play area for the school.

The rebuild removed all the parking and added a beehive-shaped spray shower guarded by two bee sculptures, hex-block paving, a community garden, play equipment, swings, a basketball court, a tennis court, benches, and oak and cherry trees.

profiles.name: Cobble Hill Park
profiles.desc: Cobble Hill Park. 172 Congress Street, Brooklyn
intro: Dutch farmers settled the area in the mid-1600s, when it was called Punkiesberg. During the Battle of Long Island in 1776 the Continental Army called it Cobble Hill, after a hill it had fortified during the Siege of Boston. The fort here, Smith's Barbette, was part of a defensive line from Gowanus Bay to Wallabout Bay.

The block between Verandah Place, Clinton Street and Henry Street once held the Weber and Whitten mansions and an empty Unitarian church. The Bohack Corporation bought the land in the late 1940s and tore down the mansions; in the early 1960s it proposed a supermarket there, and the neighborhood opposed it.

In 1962 builders bought the site to put up a six-story, 128-family apartment building. From April to July 1962 the Cobble Hill Association, the West Brooklyn Independent Democrats and neighbors gathered 1,200 signatures and petitioned the City Planning Commission, the Budget Bureau, Parks and the Mayor's Office to make it a park.
The land became City property on March 7, 1963, and Cobble Hill Park was dedicated on July 14, 1965, with trees, shrubs, game tables and a sand pit.

Parks rebuilt it in 1989 in materials that match the neighborhood's 19th-century houses: bluestone, cast iron, granite entrance columns and herringbone brick paths. The design won the Art Commission's 1988 Award for Excellence in Design and the Parks Council's first Philip Winslow Award in 1990.

By the end of his 39 years as district leader, Red Hook was known locally as "Coffeyville." Partition Street was renamed Coffey Street in 1891.

A renovation finished on July 7, 1999, paid for with $840,000 from Council Member Angel Rodriguez, $1,055,000 from Borough President Howard Golden and $24,000 from Mayor Giuliani.
The park has a spray shower, play equipment, swings, game and picnic tables, basketball and handball courts, an asphalt baseball diamond, hippopotamus animal art and crocodile-shaped benches.

intro: Named for Mother Frances Xavier Cabrini (1850-1917), founder of the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart and the first American citizen made a saint. Sent to the United States in 1889 to help Italian immigrants, she taught at parishes in Manhattan, the Bronx and at what is now Sacred Hearts and St. Stephen's Church in Brooklyn.
On this site in 1892 she opened her first school in the Northeast, St. Charles School, in a house at President and Van Brunt Streets bought by Bishop Charles E. McDonnell of Brooklyn.

It has benches, a spray shower, play equipment, and stone sculptures of an eagle and a turkey on the gateposts.

profiles.name: Nicholas Naquan Heyward Jr. Park
profiles.desc: Nicholas Naquan Heyward Jr. Park. 160 Wyckoff Street, Brooklyn
intro: Until the early 1940s three-story row houses stood here; they were torn down for the Gowanus Houses. The City took the land by condemnation in 1946, set aside the block of Hoyt, Wyckoff and Bond Streets for a park, and transferred it to Parks that year as the Gowanus Houses Playground.
Parks rebuilt the playground in 2011, and the Brooklyn Nets sponsored new basketball courts in 2017.

In 2001 it was renamed for Nicholas Naquan Heyward Jr. (1981-1994), an honor student at P.S. 20 and Nathan Hale Middle School who practiced basketball here. On September 27, 1994, while playing cops and robbers with friends using toy guns in a Gowanus Houses stairwell, he was shot by a Housing Authority police officer and died.

Each year on his birthday, August 26, the Nicholas Naquan Heyward Jr. Foundation holds a gathering here with basketball, kids' activities and a toy exchange where toy guns can be traded for books and other toys. A 1998 Groundswell mural on Baltic Street near Boerum Playground honors him.

profiles.name: Washington Park
profiles.desc: Washington Park. 1 4 Avenue, Brooklyn
intro: Once part of the ground fought over in the Battle of Brooklyn, Washington Park has a skatepark, basketball courts, a dog run, a synthetic turf field, J.J. Byrne Playground for toddlers and older kids, and the Old Stone House, now a center for Brooklyn history and the Revolution.

Parks acquired the land in 1926, and the Board of Aldermen named it J.J. Byrne Park in 1933 for James J. Byrne (1863-1930), who grew up near the Navy Yard, rose from Building Department clerk to Brooklyn Commissioner of Public Works, and was Brooklyn Borough President from 1926 until he died in office in 1930.

The Old Stone House at the back of the park reconstructs the Vechte-Cortelyou house, built by Claes Arents Vechte in 1699 and torn down around 1897. Its foundations were found in 1930, Byrne ordered it rebuilt from the original material, and it was finished in 1934 as a park office and restroom.

On August 27, 1776, in the Battle of Long Island, the Maryland 400 under Lord Stirling attacked British troops holding the house so George Washington's army could escape across Gowanus Creek. About 250 of them died.
The house later belonged to the Cortelyou family (from 1790) and Edwin C. Litchfield (from 1850), and served as the clubhouse of the Bridegrooms, the baseball team that came before the Dodgers.

In 1951 the park was joined with the new William Alexander Junior High School 51 and its playground. A full reconstruction of the Old Stone House was finished in 1996, and Parks' page reports a $10.9 million allocation to make it more accessible and upgrade it.

profiles.name: NewYork-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital
profiles.desc: NewYork-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital, 506 6th Street, Park Slope. Open 24 hours with an emergency department; Weill Cornell Medicine physicians.
profiles.addr_note: The city files the hospital lot as 269 7 Avenue
intro: NewYork-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital at 506 6th Street in Park Slope is open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with an emergency department. Its doctors are Weill Cornell Medicine physicians, and its care runs across specialties from cancer and heart care to pediatrics, women’s health and orthopedics.

The hospital lists heart care among the Top 50 Cardiovascular Hospitals in the nation, based on U.S. News & World Report’s 2024-2025 cardiology, heart and vascular surgery rankings, along with the Meyer Cancer Center, an on-site infusion therapy center and community care programs.
does: Its services: Advanced Surgery, Advanced Otolaryngology, Pulmonology, Diabetes & Endocrinology, Emergency Medicine, Interventional Radiology, Radiology, General Surgery, Bariatric Surgery, Vascular Surgery, Internal Medicine, Thoracic Surgery, Cardiothoracic Surgery, Geriatrics, Pregnancy & Maternity Care, Asthma & Other Lung Diseases, Dentistry, Cancer Care, Digestive Diseases, Heart, Neurology & Neurosurgery, Ophthalmology, Organ Transplantation, Orthopedics, Pediatrics, Psychiatry and Mental Health, Primary Care, Rehabilitation, Sleep Disorders, Spine Care, Women’s Health and Urology.

The Center for Community Health, steps from the hospital at 515 6th Street, is NYP’s outpatient building: same-day surgery, diagnostics and specialty care, from cancer treatment to women’s imaging, without an overnight stay in the hospital.

The cafeteria, in the lobby of the Carrington Pavilion, serves breakfast 7:00 to 10:30 AM and lunch 11:15 AM to 2:30 PM, and reopens 3:15 to 6:30 PM with beverages, fruit and snacks. Guest trays can be sent up to a patient’s room by calling 718-780-3401.

profiles.name: Cobble Hill Health Center
profiles.seat: Nursing and rehabilitation center · Cobble Hill
profiles.desc: Cobble Hill Health Center, 380 Henry Street, Cobble Hill. A not-for-profit nursing and rehabilitation center, part of Cobble Hill LifeCare, marking 50 years of care in 2026.
profiles.addr_note: Henry Street at Congress Street, in the Cobble Hill Historic District
intro: Cobble Hill Health Center is a nursing and rehabilitation center at 380 Henry Street, part of Cobble Hill LifeCare, a health care system for older adults, the chronically ill and people recovering from illness or a hospital stay. The center offers medical, nursing and rehabilitation services for people of all ages.
Cobble Hill Health Center, Inc. runs the center as a voluntary not-for-profit with 364 beds. 2026 marks 50 years of Cobble Hill Health Center.
does: Subacute care, a rehabilitation institute, cardiac rehabilitation, a palliative care program, long term care and Alzheimer’s care, plus in-home care through Your Choice at Home.

The building opened in 1888 as St. Peter’s Hospital, designed by J. William Schickel, and has been landmarked since 1969. After the hospital closed in 1962, the building reopened as a nursing home in 1964; a deal between the owners, Community Board 6 and the Landmarks Preservation Commission partially restored the original façade.

profiles.name: Institute for Public Architecture
profiles.seat: Design fellowship and residency · Governors Island, New York
profiles.desc: Institute for Public Architecture (IPA), the Block House, 9 Nolan Park, Governors Island. Fellowships, residencies, lectures and exhibits that use design to address social, physical and environmental inequities, including BQE2053 and the Gowanus Lab.
profiles.addr_note: Governors Island; office at 900 Broadway #802, New York, NY 10003
intro: The Institute for Public Architecture (IPA), based in the historic Block House on Governors Island, uses design to address social, physical and environmental inequities in the city through its Selected Topic Fellowship and Independent Project Residency programs, and related public lectures, exhibits and publications.
The IPA’s stated belief is in a future in which design is used as a tool for facilitating social justice and the public has a voice in all decisions that shape the built environment.
does: The Independent Project Residency is an eleven week live-in residency at the Block House for emerging and mid-career practitioners whose work focuses on the public realm; the 2027 open call is up on its site.

For CB6 the relevant work is BQE2053, the IPA’s project on the future of the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, including a screening of The Story of the BQE at Brooklyn Borough Hall in October 2026 with a panel on alternatives to freight on the BQE, and Echo Archive: Gowanus Lab, a 2025 Fall Residency project.
kv: Selected Topic Fellowship; Independent Project Residency

profiles.name: Gowanus Oversight Task Force
profiles.desc: Gowanus Oversight Task Force (GOTF): the volunteer, community-based group formed under the Gowanus rezoning's 56 Points of Agreement to track each commitment and hold quarterly public meetings with city agencies.
profiles.addr_note: The Gowanus rezoning area; meetings are announced on gowanustaskforce.net
intro: The Gowanus Oversight Task Force works proactively and collaboratively with New York City agencies to advance timely and equitable implementation of the commitments detailed in the 56 Points of Agreement (POA) from the Gowanus rezoning, as well as community goals outlined in the Gowanus Neighborhood Plan.

Formed as part of Commitment 1, the Task Force is a volunteer, community-based group that keeps an online repository tracking each commitment’s status and holds quarterly public meetings to promote accountability, transparency and continued engagement with the Gowanus community.
does: At the quarterly public meetings the public hears directly from city agencies on the status of the City’s commitments, submits questions about the POA and exchanges information about advancements in Gowanus; past meeting materials and registration for upcoming ones are on its site.

Its resources include the Gowanus Commitment Tracker, the Points of Agreement and their summary, the POA map, the Gowanus Racial Equity Report and fact sheets on the DEP and EPA CSO tank site and on the state Brownfield and federal Superfund programs. The Task Force recruits new committee members each fall.
kv: Commitment 1 of the 56 Points of Agreement

profiles.name: Urban Meadow Community Garden
profiles.seat: GreenThumb community garden · Columbia Street Waterfront District, Brooklyn
profiles.desc: The Urban Meadow, the volunteer-run NYC Parks GreenThumb community garden at the corner of President Street and Van Brunt Street in the Columbia Street Waterfront District, Brooklyn, opened in 2008 on the site of the former Mother Cabrini Chapel. Its annual Halloween party and parade, membership, calendar and contact.
profiles.addr: President Street at Van Brunt Street
profiles.addr_note: The corner of President and Van Brunt Streets, across from Mother Cabrini Park
intro: The Urban Meadow is a volunteer-run community garden at the corner of President Street and Van Brunt Street in the Columbia Street Waterfront District, licensed through NYC Parks’ GreenThumb program and entirely operated and maintained by the neighbors who tend it.

The lot once held the Mother Cabrini Chapel, demolished after the sewer reconstruction of the 1970s; the Parks Department acquired it in 2000. Landscape designer Julie Farris, who had turned a nearby lot into a temporary pasture in 2005, pushed for a permanent green space, and the roughly 8,000-square-foot meadow of flowering dogwoods and wildflowers opened with a ribbon cutting on June 11, 2008, a project of XS Space and Balmori Associates with the Parks Department, the Borough President’s office and Brooklyn Community Board 6.
does: The Halloween Parade. Every year on or around Halloween the garden throws a Halloween party and parade from Mother Cabrini Park and Playground, across the street: costumes, a brass band leading a procession through the neighborhood, coffee and baked treats before and pizza after, by donation, and games for the kids afterward. In 2026 it is Saturday, October 31, 11:30 AM to 1:30 PM, with the Underground Horns leading the procession at noon and a new carved and decorated pumpkin contest for kids 12 and under and for adults.

Membership and open days. The garden is run by its members and coordinators; 2026 membership requests go through their form, and open garden events, markets and concerts are posted on their calendar and Instagram.

going.kicker: Saturday, October 31, 11:30 AM to 1:30 PM · Mother Cabrini Park and Playground
going.title: Urban Meadow Halloween Party and Parade
going.text: Costumes on. The Underground Horns brass band leads the procession through the neighborhood at noon. New this year, a bring-your-own carved or decorated pumpkin contest, kids 12 and under and adults, with prizes for the best; bring your pumpkin to the Urban Meadow before the parade and register in advance. Coffee and baked treats before, pizza after, by donation, then games and activities for the kids and a costume portrait station.

profiles.name: New Yorkers for Parks
profiles.seat: Parks advocacy organization · citywide, based in Lower Manhattan
profiles.desc: New Yorkers for Parks, the citywide parks advocacy organization founded in 1908 from the Brooklyn Society for Parks and Playgrounds: its research on open space by community board, the Play Fair for Parks coalition, the Daffodil Project, the Let Red Hook Swim campaign, and how to reach it.
profiles.addr_note: Mailing address: PO Box 431, New York, NY 10272
intro: New Yorkers for Parks is the city’s parks advocacy organization. It works with local communities, public officials and advocates on the creation, protection and care of New York City’s parks and open spaces.
It began in 1908, when the Brooklyn Society for Parks and Playgrounds merged with two other groups, and took the name New Yorkers for Parks in 2002.
does: It produces research on the city’s open space: Open Space Profiles for every community board, the Open Space Index, City Council district profiles and the Report Card on Parks series. Its 2021 profile of Brooklyn Community Board 6 covers Park Slope, Carroll Gardens, Gowanus and Red Hook.

It co-founded the Play Fair for Parks coalition, more than 400 members, with the New York League of Conservation Voters and District Council 37, calling for greater city investment in the parks system, and runs campaigns such as Fix the Basics: Fund Parks Now, NYC Needs Car-Free Parks, Fix the Bathrooms and Drinking Fountains, and Let Red Hook Swim, to reopen Red Hook Pool and invest in public pools citywide.

Each fall it runs the Daffodil Project, distributing free daffodil bulbs and native seeds to volunteers in every borough as a living memorial to the victims of September 11. The project began in 2001.
profiles.does_title: What New Yorkers for Parks does

profiles.name: Transportation Alternatives
profiles.seat: Street safety and transportation advocacy · citywide, with a Brooklyn activist committee
profiles.desc: Transportation Alternatives, the citywide advocacy organization founded in 1973 for people who walk, bike and ride transit: its Brooklyn activist committee, its campaigns in and around Brooklyn Community Board 6 (Bergen and Dean bike boulevards, 4th Avenue, a Red Hook bus to Manhattan, Prospect Park connections), and how to reach it.
intro: Transportation Alternatives is a 501(c)(3) advocacy organization founded in 1973 that works in all five boroughs on transportation policy, traffic safety and street access for people walking, biking and riding transit. Its stated mission is to reclaim New York City from cars and make its streets safe, sustainable and equitable places to walk, bike, take transit and gather.

Staff and volunteer activists run twenty or more local and citywide campaigns at a time. Volunteer committees meet monthly in the Bronx and Uptown, Brooklyn, North Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and Staten Island, with a youth committee as well. It also runs Families for Safe Streets, founded in 2014 for people injured or bereaved by traffic crashes.
does: The Brooklyn Activist Committee meets every fourth Thursday at 6:30 PM, in person with an occasional call-in option; its organizer is Rose Uscianowski, and the committee can be reached at brooklyn@transalt.org.

Its campaigns in and around the district include Build the Bergen and Dean Bike Boulevards, with the Bergen Bike Bus and a coalition urging NYC DOT to build the corridors; Fix 4th Avenue; a Red Hook bus to Manhattan in the MTA’s Brooklyn bus network redesign; Build the Park Slope Pedestrian Plaza, to make the temporary open street permanent; and Prospect Park Connections, protected bike connections and pedestrian safety around the park.
Citywide campaigns include $3 Citi Bike, Slower Safer Speeds Now (20 mph limits under Sammy’s Law), No Gaps in the Bike Network, NYCiclovia and Expand Student OMNY.
profiles.does_title: In and around Brooklyn Community Board 6

profiles.name: Riders Alliance
profiles.seat: Membership organization of bus and subway riders · citywide, based in Lower Manhattan
profiles.desc: Riders Alliance, the membership organization of New York City bus and subway riders formed in 2012: Fix the Bus, Fair Fares, Six Minute Service, congestion pricing, the Fix the Bus Brooklyn Assembly, and how to reach it.
intro: Riders Alliance is a membership organization of bus and subway riders dedicated to winning better transit in New York City. Formed in 2012, it organizes riders to identify transit issues, hold elected officials accountable and lobby for reliable, affordable public transit; its early wins included service improvements on the C, G and R lines in Brooklyn.
does: Fix the Bus calls for fast, free and fully funded buses: busways, bus shelters, countdown clocks and all-door boarding. Its Fix the Bus Brooklyn Assembly is Tuesday, December 8, 2026, 6:00 to 7:30 PM, at the Brooklyn Public Library’s Central Branch, for bus riders to meet and start organizing in their neighborhoods.

Fair Fares won half-price transit fares for low-income New Yorkers, and in 2026 the largest expansion of Fair Fares eligibility, covering over a million New Yorkers. The alliance also campaigned for congestion pricing and for Six Minute Service, which won more frequent subway service and new transit operating revenue in 2023.
With the Pratt Center for Community Development it published Better Buses for Flatbush Avenue, a participatory research report on bus service on Flatbush Avenue.

profiles.name: New York League of Conservation Voters
profiles.seat: Statewide environmental political organization · based in Lower Manhattan
profiles.desc: The New York League of Conservation Voters, the non-partisan statewide environmental organization that lobbies, scores lawmakers on its State and City Environmental Scorecards, endorses candidates and works to elect them: its New York City priorities and how to reach it.
intro: The New York League of Conservation Voters describes itself as the only statewide environmental organization in New York that fights for clean water, clean air, renewable energy and open space through political action. It is non-partisan.
does: It sets annual policy priorities, lobbies, and evaluates lawmakers through its New York State and New York City Environmental Scorecards. It endorses candidates based on questionnaires, interviews by regional boards and scorecard records, and through two political action committees, NYLCV Gives Green and the NYLCV Victory Fund, works to elect them.

Its New York City priorities include low-emission transportation, conserving parks and natural areas, and waste management toward the city’s Zero Waste goal. With New Yorkers for Parks and District Council 37 it co-founded the Play Fair for Parks coalition. Its public events are run by the affiliated NYLCV Education Fund.

profiles.name: New York Legal Assistance Group
profiles.seat: Free civil legal services · citywide, based in Lower Manhattan
profiles.desc: NYLAG, the New York Legal Assistance Group, founded in 1989: free civil legal services for New Yorkers experiencing poverty or in crisis, LegalHealth in hospitals and clinics, tenant representation under Right to Counsel in Brooklyn, Manhattan and Queens, immigration help, and how to reach it.
intro: NYLAG, the New York Legal Assistance Group, uses the law to help New Yorkers experiencing poverty or in crisis: free civil legal services, financial empowerment, impact litigation, policy advocacy and community partnerships. It was formed in 1989.
does: Its Tenants’ Rights work represents tenants facing eviction under New York City’s Right to Counsel law, in Brooklyn, Manhattan and Queens.

LegalHealth brings free legal help into hospitals and clinics for New Yorkers with serious or chronic health problems and financial hardship, pairing lawyers with medical teams; its program areas include cancer, immigration, standby guardianship and veterans, plus training for health care providers.
Its Immigrant Protection Unit gives low-income immigrants consultation and representation: naturalization, adjustment of status, VAWA self-petitions, U visas, asylum and removal defense.

profiles.name: New York Immigration Coalition
profiles.seat: Immigrant and refugee rights coalition · statewide, based in Midtown Manhattan
profiles.desc: The New York Immigration Coalition, founded in 1987: an umbrella policy and advocacy organization for more than 200 immigrant and refugee rights groups across New York State, its campaigns (New York for All, Access to Representation, Our City Our Vote, Coverage4All, Language Access), Know Your Rights resources, and how to reach it.
intro: The New York Immigration Coalition (NYIC) is an umbrella policy and advocacy organization that represents more than 200 immigrant and refugee rights groups throughout New York: grassroots and nonprofit community organizations, religious and academic institutions, labor unions, and legal and socioeconomic justice organizations. It was founded in 1987.

A state-wide, member-led coalition, NYIC works to transform the lives of all New Yorkers by strengthening and building its members’ power, and using their collective voice to advocate for opportunity and justice.
does: Immigrant rights. NYIC works at the city, state and federal levels to expand access to counsel and status and to end cooperation between local police and federal immigration enforcement. Its campaigns include New York for All, which would prohibit state and local officers from enforcing federal immigration law and bar ICE and CBP from non-public areas of state and local property without a judicial warrant; the Access to Representation Act, with the Vera Institute and I-ARC, to guarantee a lawyer for immigrants at risk of deportation in New York; Dignity Not Detention; and ICE Out of NYC.

Civic participation. NYIC runs the New Citizen Voter Registration Project, the largest voter registration project in New York State, voter education on rights inside and outside the voting booth, and Our City, Our Vote, its campaign to expand municipal voting rights for immigrants living in New York City.

Education, health and language. NYIC works to improve education for immigrant families and students, to advance immigrants’ access to quality health care (Coverage4All), and on Language Access, Legal Service Funding, Welcoming New York and the state Office for New Americans.
Know Your Rights. NYIC publishes resources on your rights as a New Yorker and how to access help, including a guide to immigration legal services in Brooklyn.
kv: More than 200 immigrant and refugee rights groups across New York State

intro: Kentler International Drawing Space is a nonprofit gallery at 353 Van Brunt Street in Red Hook devoted to drawings and works on paper. Florence Neal and Scott Pfaffman opened it in April 1990.

profiles.addr_note: Between Third and Fourth Avenues. R to Union Street.
intro: The Textile Arts Center at 505 Carroll Street in Gowanus is dedicated to raising awareness and understanding of textiles through creative educational programming for kids and adults.

On the calendar: the Give Back Market and Tat & Chat with the Brooklyn Lace Guild.

profiles.name: The Green-Wood Cemetery
profiles.seat: Cemetery and National Historic Landmark · Greenwood Heights, Brooklyn
profiles.desc: The Green-Wood Cemetery, 500 25th Street, Brooklyn. The Green-Wood Cemetery was founded in 1838 as a rural cemetery by Henry Evelyn Pierrepont and David Bates Douglass, its engineer and landscape architect. It covers 478 acres, with the mai
profiles.addr_note: Main entrance at Fifth Avenue and 25th Street
intro: The Green-Wood Cemetery was founded in 1838 as a rural cemetery by Henry Evelyn Pierrepont and David Bates Douglass, its engineer and landscape architect. It covers 478 acres, with the main entrance at Fifth Avenue and 25th Street, just south of CB6 in Brooklyn Community Board 7.

It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 2006. Battle Hill, the highest natural point in Brooklyn, is named for fighting there in the Battle of Brooklyn on August 27, 1776. About 570,000 people are buried there.
does: Green-Wood is a working nonprofit cemetery. The Green-Wood Historic Fund, a separate nonprofit, supports its preservation and public programs: tours, talks, concerts and family events.
On the calendar: its public events, such as the Day of the Dead family celebration.

intro: Dzieci Theatre is an experimental ensemble founded in 1997, directed by founding director Matt Mitler with co-founder Yvonne Brecht. It works in the tradition of Jerzy Grotowski and describes every show as a quest for deeper meaning.
does: Dzieci brings its work into hospitals and institutions serving people in need, working alongside health care professionals. Its Fools Mass, a comedy of medieval fools holding a mass, has played around New York City since 1998, including at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine.
On the calendar: the Garfield Place Black Light Halloween Puppet Show.

profiles.name: Brooklyn Creative Reuse
profiles.seat: Creative reuse center · Industry City, Sunset Park, Brooklyn
profiles.desc: Brooklyn Creative Reuse, a nonprofit creative reuse center at Industry City: secondhand art and craft supplies, what it accepts as donations, store hours, classes, mending circles and swaps, and how to reach it.
profiles.addr_note: Industry City, 2nd floor. Open to the public, no appointment needed.
intro: Brooklyn Creative Reuse is a creative reuse center that helps divert discarded arts materials from the landfill so they are reimagined and repurposed. In its own words, Brooklyn Creative Reuse is dedicated to a more creative and sustainable Brooklyn.

Stephanie O’Brien launched Brooklyn Creative Reuse in December 2024. After a first year of pop-ups, the store opened at Industry City in spring 2026. Brooklyn Creative Reuse is a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit, run largely by volunteers.
does: The store. Donated art and craft supplies, resold at affordable prices. Open Wednesday and Thursday, 2 PM to 7 PM, and Friday through Sunday, 11 AM to 6 PM.

Donations. Brooklyn Creative Reuse accepts adhesives, art books, ceramics and sculpture supplies, drawing and illustration supplies, fabrics and fibers, hardware, jewelry supplies, office supplies, paint and brushes, paper and canvas, and scrapbook items. Brooklyn Creative Reuse does not accept bedding, pillows, clothes, outdoor lighting or decorations, luggage, unlabeled liquids, furniture or household items.
Classes, mending circles and swaps. Workshops taught by teaching artists, a free mending circle series, and craft supply swaps and pop-ups with libraries and community organizations across Brooklyn.
kv: Wednesday and Thursday, 2 PM to 7 PM; Friday through Sunday, 11 AM to 6 PM

profiles.name: Citizens Committee for New York City
profiles.seat: Microgrants for neighborhood leaders · citywide, based in Harlem
profiles.desc: The Citizens Committee for New York City (CitizensNYC), founded in 1975: grants of up to $5,000 for local leaders, community groups and small businesses across the five boroughs, the Community Leaders Grant and the Neighborhood Business Grant, and how to reach it.
profiles.addr_note: Mail goes to 30 East 125th Street, #189, New York, NY 10035.
intro: The Citizens Committee for New York City, known as CitizensNYC, is one of New York’s oldest microgranting organizations. Founded in 1975, CitizensNYC funds and supports everyday New Yorkers working to improve their communities, from block parties to environmental resilience.
CitizensNYC’s grantee partners include more than 500 grassroots leaders, community groups and neighborhood organizations across the five boroughs.
does: Grants of up to $5,000 for local leaders, community groups and small businesses making a difference in their neighborhoods.
Community Leaders Grants go to resident-led groups and neighborhood projects. Questions go to grants@citizensnyc.org.
Neighborhood Business Grants go to small businesses. Questions go to businessgrants@citizensnyc.org.
Office hours. CitizensNYC holds virtual office hours on Zoom for anyone with questions about a grant or an application.
kv: More than 500 across the five boroughs

profiles.desc: Tony Simone, Assembly Member · State Assembly District 75. Assembly Member Tony Simone represents State Assembly District 75. It sits in Manhattan.
intro: Community boards: Manhattan 4, 5, 7
Assembly Member Tony Simone represents State Assembly District 75. It sits in Manhattan.
The district overlaps community boards Manhattan 4 and Manhattan 5.
It is policed by the 10th, 13th, 14th, 18th and 22nd Precincts.
It overlaps council districts 3, 4 and 6 and Senate districts 28 and 47.
Members of the State Assembly serve two year terms.
Re-elected on November 3, 2026. The new term starts January 1, 2027. Next on the ballot in November 2028.

Through interactiveworkshops and concerts, LAC uses music as a basis for social and emotional learning, understanding and integrating empathy, and cultivating toleranceand openness to new ideas. Using music to engage and entertain, the teaching artists of LAC connect their programs to the school curricula and meetNew York State education standards at all times. intro: Hebrew Free Loan Society is a human and social services organization in Manhattan that the New York City Council has funded.

In its own words, to the IRS: The hebrew free loan society (hfls) fosters economic stability and opportunity for lower-income new yorkers through interest-free lending. Hfls loans make an immediate, concrete difference in the lives of our borrowers, enabling them to invest in their education, start a business, build a family and meet emergency expenses. Hfls is non-sectarian; our borrowers represent New York's diverse jewish and non-jewish communities. Since its founding in 1892 hfls has provided over $300 million in loans to more than 875,000 borrowers while maintaining a repayment rate of 99%. As hfls loans are repaid, the capital is lent out again and again, helping more people and multiplying the impact over time.

profiles.name: Henry Street Settlement

In its own words, to the IRS: Founded in 1893 by social reformer lillian wald, henry street settlement's mission is to open doors of opportunity to enrich lives and enhance human progress for lower east side residents and other new yorkers through social services, arts, and health care programs. As one of the nation's first settlement houses, henry street's approach to human services has always been place-based and participant-inclusive, designed to meet the full spectrum of human needs and evolving to effectively serve changing community priorities. This approach, which is as relevant today as it was 132 years ago, is reflected in all of our programs that reach more than 50,000 people annually across 18 program sites throughout the lower east side.

In its own words, to the IRS: see schedule O for continuation of statement. The United Methodist City Society (UMCS) is a multifaceted program agency that is the urban social service program partner of United Methodist churches in the New York metropolitan area. The UMCS was founded in 1838 by Methodist Women in New York City for the purpose of organizing charity schools among the poor. In its own words, to the IRS: The rubin museum of art in chelsea, New York city, explores and celebrates himalayan art, cultures, and ideas across history and into the present. With its globally renowned collection, centered largely around art from the tibetan plateau, the rubin fosters understanding and appreciation of himalayan art by interpreting and relating it to our shared human experience today. Inspired by the tenets of buddhism, hinduism, and indigenous religions, and aligned with ongoing research into learning, behavior, and the brain, the rubin offers innovative exhibitions and programs that examine provocative ideas across the arts and explore the mind. Uwnyc serves approximately 1 million New York city residents struggling to make ends meet, as well as the agencies, organizations, partners, and institutions that serve them. profiles.name: Exalt Youth
profiles.desc: Exalt Youth, youth development organization funded by the NYC Council.
intro: Exalt Youth is a youth development organization in Manhattan that the New York City Council has funded.

In its own words, to the IRS: Exalt youth serves youth involved in the criminal justice system, moving them away from incarceration towards re-engagement with education and meaningful job opportunities. Our students come from some of the most economically depressed neighborhoods in New York and are often facing potentially life altering circumstances. The exalt mission combines a rigorous curriculum with paid internships and career development to elevate expectations of personal success for court-involved youth ages 15-19. Exalt tracks participant outcomes in three specific areas: 1) criminal justice avoidance; 2) academic progression; and 3) employability. Our model is built upon our tested incubation period at the blue ridge foundation in 2006 and gold star evaluation by john jay research and evaluation center in 2013.

We envision a country of young people working as active and effective citizens to collectively rebuild our american democracy. Gc teaches teenagers how to take effective political action. Through an innovative in-class curriculum, students work with local leaders to fix local problems. Through this real-world experience,our teens are building an active democracy. Our innovative, action-based program will revolutionize civics education in this country. Generation citizen is building a new generation of youth activists and leaders; a generation inspired and equipped to make change.

In its own words, to the IRS: Colony-south brooklyn houses' mission is to offer humanitarian services to the disadvantaged people in the borough of brooklyn, NY. Since 1904, colony-south has provided numerous social and educational programs for underprivileged children and their families, many of whom have experienced homelessness, unemployment, and a variety of developmental and emotional difficulties. Colony-south operates under the policy that people who are ill-clothed and ill-housed cannot find work and people who are uneducated cannot reach their potential as human beings. For over a century, colony has dedicated itself to helping all of its diverse clients empower themselves, take charge of their lives and build stable futures for their families. Colony-south continues to champion those less fortunate, as they climb the ladder from welfare to work and become productive, contributing members of their communities.

intro: South Bronx Overall Economic Development is a community and economic development organization in Bronx that the New York City Council has funded.

In its own words, to the IRS: Our mission is to enhance the quality of life in the south bronx by strengthening businesses and creating innovative economic, housing, educational, and career development programs for youth and adults. Sobro was founded in 1972 by a group of business executives and community leaders. Our task was urgent: reverse the flight of businesses and jobs from the south bronx. It was the first and most fundamental step toward rebuilding a community whose name evoked images of burned buildings, crime, poverty and drugs. But as sobro began to evolve, it became clearer that community revitalization required a multi-faceted effort. Today, we address all aspects of community development: assisting businesses to get started and grow, training residents according to the needs of employers, offering opportunities for youth to learn and develop, and creating affordable housing and commercial spaces that reverse blight in the community.

As of July 1, 2017, Lavelle Prep is a school within the newly merged Integration Charter School (ICS) network. In its own words: “Public School 255 was originally named for William E. Kelly. William E. Kelly (1872-1929) was the postmaster for our school’s area and was acknowledged nationally as a dutiful civil servant. In 1994, the Board of Education rededicated it in honor of Barbara Reing (1933-1992). Ms. Reing worked as a teacher and a supervisor of special education at P.S. 255 for nearly 20 years. Ms. Reing worked tirelessly on mainstreaming her students, years before the concept became popular. Ms. Reing sadly died of cancer in 1992. She had worked until a week before she passed away.”

groups.name: Schools, parks and facilities
topics: Courts, fields, pools and recreation centers

about: group puts each organization under one of four headings in the apps' Organizations tab (Community groups, Local businesses, Elected officials, Government agencies); topic is the subsection within Community groups and Local businesses; sort orders officials and agencies (local first). groups sets the headings and the order of their subsections. Change these here and the apps follow, no build. Local businesses are profiles with group Local businesses; their topic is the business improvement district they are in (or their neighborhood when outside one), and the BID itself heads that subsection with sort -2 or -1. businesses and businessOrgs keep the earlier copies. Government agencies beyond the local ones come from data/agencies.json (the nyc.gov agency directory, as on bkcb6.app/agencies) with locations from data/agency-locations.json, written by scripts/build_orgs_agencies.py; they carry from: agencies.json and are rewritten each run. Every business in the CB6 business directory is a profile too (slug biz-*, scripts/biz_profiles.py), under Local businesses by kind, with its district in seat. Schools, libraries, child care, parks, hospitals and health care, and gyms and athletic facilities are profiles too (slug place-*, scripts/places_profiles.py), under Schools, parks and facilities.

intro: The Jalopy Theatre and School of Music is an arts space showcasing folk and traditional music and art from New York City, the Americas and the world. Jalopy calls itself the only home for folk and traditional music and art in New York City.
Husband and wife Geoff and Lynette Wiley founded Jalopy in 2006. Jalopy has joined forces with Living Traditions, the nonprofit founded in 1994 that produced KlezKamp.

intro: Principles GI Coffee House is inspired by the egalitarian, antiwar coffeehouses of the Vietnam War era. Principles is a community and event space that is also a cafe, run by owner Katie Bishop at 139 9th Street.
